strengths: Addresses a genuine and practical limitation of prior anomaly-generation work: the paper correctly identifies that few-shot anomaly generation (FSAG) requires real anomalous samples, which contradicts the motivation for generation in the first place, and targets the more useful zero-shot setting.

The core idea of delta-denoising attribution (contrasting per-step denoiser outputs of a normal-prompt and anomaly-prompt branch under a shared schedule to build an image-specific localization mask) is a reasonable and relatively novel adaptation of DiffEdit-style mask derivation to the anomaly domain, going beyond low-resolution cross-attention masks used by AnomalyAny.

The additional components (normal-reference guided initialization, token-level prompt refinement with anomaly-semantic distillation and context alignment, spatially-biased cross-attention) are individually simple and well-motivated, and the paper provides both qualitative (Fig. 4-5) and quantitative (Table 3) ablations showing each module's contribution.

Experiments cover generation quality (IS/IC-LPIPS), downstream detection utility (AUROC/AP at image and pixel level), and qualitative comparisons on both MVTec AD and unseen categories, which is a reasonably comprehensive evaluation for the claimed contribution type.

The paper is transparent about the unfair comparison with FSAG methods that leak test-set anomalies during fine-tuning, and appropriately frames AnomalyAny as the primary competitor, which strengthens the credibility of the empirical claims.

The controllability aspect (steering defect type/severity through the descriptive anchor in Lanom) is a nice added capability that few zero-shot generation methods offer, illustrated convincingly in Fig. 5.
weaknesses: Downstream detection results are mixed rather than uniformly better than the main ZSAG baseline: several categories (e.g., cable, capsule, grid, toothbrush, transistor, zipper) show DeltaDeno underperforming AnomalyAny on AUCi/APi, and pixel-level AP averages are lower than even AnoGen/AnoDiff (though those leak test data). The paper's narrative slightly understates this category-level variance.

The method has many hyperparameters (γ, τmid, τfinal, β, λ, η, step size αt, number of prompt-refinement iterations) whose sensitivity is not analyzed; without a hyperparameter/robustness study, reproducibility and generalization to new domains beyond MVTec-like textures remain uncertain despite the promise of code release.

Only one true zero-shot baseline (AnomalyAny) is compared against; the ZSAG literature landscape is still small, but the empirical claims of "zero-shot SOTA" would be more convincing with additional zero-shot or training-free baselines (e.g., simple DiffEdit/SDEdit adaptations) to isolate how much benefit comes from the anomaly-specific design versus generic mask-guided editing.

No computational cost / inference-time comparison is provided, even though the method runs two synchronized diffusion branches plus iterative prompt-refinement optimization, attention biasing, and SAM-based foreground extraction — this added overhead relative to AnomalyAny or single-branch methods is not quantified.

Evaluation metrics (IS, IC-LPIPS) are relatively weak proxies for photorealism/localization quality, and the paper's own limitations section acknowledges this; no user study or MLLM-based assessment is included to substantiate the qualitative realism claims quantitatively.

Results on datasets beyond MVTec AD are deferred entirely to the appendix (not provided here), limiting the ability to judge cross-domain generalization claims made prominently in the abstract and introduction from the main text alone.

The technical novelty relative to DiffEdit (contrasting source/target prompts under shared schedule to derive an edit mask) is somewhat incremental; the paper would benefit from a more explicit discussion of what is fundamentally new in the attribution mechanism versus adapting an existing editing paradigm to a new application.
